name: ICAN (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a nuclear war kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: ICAN (Geneva), the coalition of over 700 groups behind the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, campaigns for states to join the treaty and against nuclear deterrence, nuclear weapons spending and investment in the weapons' producers; this model covers all its programmes in 2024 (CHF 2.2M, $2.5M spent), the latest year with audited accounts. At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, from {{low}} to {{high}} on its plausible range: the campaign is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of nuclear war (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts) at 0.3 of a typical project's effect, and the treaty's implementation and the year's four new states parties through the treaty's cut, which we judge at a tenth of what typical nuclear work would achieve with the resources spent on the treaty because no nuclear-armed or allied state has joined it. Its work is aimed at states without nuclear weapons and at publics rather than at the decisions of nuclear-armed governments. The biggest uncertainties are how much a dollar of nuclear work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; ten times either way) and how much the treaty does at all (from all but nothing to as much as typical work), so the result is mostly uncertainty. Every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured.

rows.label: TPNW: everyone's resources spent on the treaty itself, 2010-2024 ($ million)
rows.explainer: Everyone's spending and time on the treaty itself (its negotiation, entry into force, universalisation and implementation) from the humanitarian-impact initiative (2010) to the end of 2024, leaving out the deterrence, divestment and spending campaigns valued in the field work. ICAN: its reported operating expenses were CHF 1.82 million in 2021, 2.80 million in 2022, 2.57 million in 2023 and 2.21 million in 2024 (2022 report p. 29, https://assets.nationbuilder.com/ican/pages/3180/attachments/original/1677846259/ICAN_2022_Annual_report_web.pdf; 2023 report, https://assets.nationbuilder.com/ican/pages/4012/attachments/original/1715180542/ICAN_2023_AnnualReport_April24_Audited_web.pdf; 2024 report p. 29), with a CHF 1.2 million budget in its 2019 report (p. 21); about CHF 8 million judged for 2010-2018 and 2020, so about $20 million in all, about 70% of it on the treaty itself (the 2019 budget's entry-into-force and cities-and-parliaments shares, 42%, plus implementation since): about $14 million. Partners' and the Red Cross movement's treaty work (PAX, WILPF's Reaching Critical Will, Article 36, Norwegian People's Aid, IPPNW and national campaigns): about $35 million. Governments' diplomats and conferences (the three humanitarian-impact conferences of 2013-2014, the 2017 negotiations, three meetings of states parties): about $50 million. About $100 million, our rough count, from $50 million to $300 million. It sets the scale of a typical project's cut the treaty is measured against (pol_relative_cut).

rows.label: TPNW: its cut in the risk per dollar behind it, as a multiple of a typical project's
rows.explainer: How much the treaty cuts the risk of nuclear war per dollar spent on it, against Rethink Priorities' typical small nuclear project. Its path to the risk is the legal norm its membership and meetings carry: a ban on possession, use and threat that delegitimises deterrence. None of the nine nuclear-armed states, and none of the states that host their weapons or endorse their use in their defence, has joined (pp. 8-9); none has changed an arsenal or doctrine because of it; it binds only states without weapons. Even where publics back it the norm hasn't moved an allied government: 75% of Japanese adults back joining, and in the researchers' survey experiment the government's security and non-proliferation arguments didn't shift them, yet Japan stays out (Baron, Gibbons and Herzog 2020). Divestment and allied publics are valued in the field work, not here. Anchors from the humanitarian-disarmament treaties: at the high end, the United States, outside the Mine Ban Treaty, adopted in 2014 a policy of not using anti-personnel mines outside Korea, reversed in 2020 and restored in 2022 (Congressional Research Service, U.S. Anti-Personnel Landmine Use Policy, https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF11440.html); at the low end, the same state announced cluster munitions for Ukraine on 7 July 2023 despite the Convention on Cluster Munitions (https://www.opb.org/article/2023/07/07/the-u-s-is-sending-cluster-bombs-to-ukraine-despite-humanitarian-warnings/), and nuclear deterrence is far more central to those states' security than mines or cluster munitions. 0.1 (0.01, all but nothing, to 1, as effective as typical work): a tenth of a typical project, our judgment, so the treaty's whole cut equals about $10 million of typical nuclear work. Harm beyond a typical project's backfire (friction with the Non-Proliferation Treaty) is in hazard_harm_share.

rows.label: TPNW: one of the year's new parties' weight against the average party
rows.explainer: Each new party is first given the average party's share of the treaty (÷ tpnw_states_parties). Two pulls on that: the treaty needed 50 ratifications to exist in law, so much of its norm came with the first 50, and three of the four 2024 joiners (São Tomé and Príncipe, Sierra Leone, the Solomon Islands) are small states outside any alliance, whose joining adds less than the average; Indonesia, the largest party (about 280 million of the parties' 2.5 billion people, p. 9) and a G20 member, adds more. 0.6 (0.25 to 1.5), our judgment.

rows.label: Policy win: share of the yearly nuclear risk one new state party removes while in force
rows.explainer: The template's calibration: everyone's resources spent on the treaty (tpnw_resources_musd) × a typical $1 million's cut in the nuclear catastrophe risk (@catastrophe.nuclear_catastrophe_cut_per_million) × the treaty's multiple of a typical project (tpnw_vs_typical) is the whole treaty's cut, about 0.36% of the yearly risk; one new state party adds its share (÷ tpnw_states_parties) at a marginal party's weight (tpnw_marginal_party_weight), about 0.003%. Shared by count of states, not by population, since a state's vote and signature carry the norm; Indonesia's size is in the weight. The extinction-level size is cut in the same proportion as a typical project's (pol_deaths_per_year), so each new party equals about $0.08 million of typical work (100 × 0.1 × 0.6 ÷ 73).

rows.label: Nuclear field work: share that is the treaty's implementation (valued at the treaty's multiple)
rows.explainer: Of the field work, the share whose effect runs through the treaty itself: the meetings of states parties and their intersessional work, briefings for diplomats, the coordination committee's retreat and the workshop with the nuclear-weapon-free zones (the report's 'Implementing the Nuclear Ban Treaty' pages, pp. 12-13, about 5-10% of its pages on the year's work, pp. 6-27). 15% (5% to 40%), our judgment: above the pages' share because the Geneva staff's diplomatic work on the meetings and the coordination committee fills more of the year than its pages show; valued at the treaty's own multiple (tpnw_vs_typical), the rest at nuclear_campaign_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: how far the typical project's effect applies to the campaign outside the treaty
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small nuclear project applies to ICAN's campaigning outside the treaty: the deterrence and spending work, divestment, research, media and the partner network. Its outputs are many and public (714 partners in 110 countries, 131 financial institutions with policies against the weapons, investors in producers down from 306 to 287, a widely cited spending report) and some reach investors, parliaments and publics in nuclear-armed and allied states, but no arsenal, doctrine or budget is shown to have moved (spending rose about 11% in 2024 by its own report, Hidden Costs, https://www.icanw.org/hidden_costs_2024_global_nuclear_weapons_spending), and divestment touches producers paid by governments. Well below typical: 0.3 (0.05 to 1), our judgment.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: A weighted blend (Convention 7): the treaty's implementation at the treaty's own multiple of a typical project (tpnw_vs_typical), the rest of the campaign at nuclear_campaign_evidence_adj, so each path to the risk has one home: the legal norm and its meetings in the treaty's multiple, investors and publics in the campaign's.

rows.label: Policy win: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: 1: the new parties' cut is judged directly (pol_relative_cut, through the treaty's multiple of a typical project), so the doubt about whether the treaty works is there, not here. 0.8 to 1.2 for whether the four new parties implement it (national laws, reporting).

rows.explainer: Whether the four governments would have joined in 2024 on their own timetables without the campaign: Indonesia had signed in 2017 and its parliament passed the ratification law in 2024 after years of steps of its own; the African conference and country meetings target exactly such pending ratifications, and the report credits ICAN and its partners with an important role (p. 9). Others' lobbying is in pol_attribution_share_shared, not here. 0.6 (0.3 to 0.85), our judgment; that they would have joined some years later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted, each part a share of the modelled value: a norm against any use also lowers the chance of a single detonation or a limited nuclear war, which kills far fewer than 10% of people and has no shared forecast (nuclear_smaller_per_year 0), 8%; the nuclear-justice work (other_cost_share: recognition, victim assistance and remediation for people harmed by testing), 2%. 10% (0 to 30%), our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut per dollar (Rethink Priorities' backfire step). Campaigning for a ban can't speed up any capability. 0, down to −5%, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: backlash beyond a typical project's, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): critics argue the treaty splits the states of the Non-Proliferation Treaty and that pressing allies to leave extended deterrence could push some towards weapons of their own; none is shown to happen (the 2022 review conference failed over Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia plant, not the ban), and ICAN publishes no technical weapons detail. 0, down to −10%, because the treaty is contested among the states it wants to persuade. Our judgment.
